scores.why: The claim instruction checks the proof's terms and beneficiary, calls the hard-coded RISC Zero verifier and pays in the same instruction; no sponsor signature, no admin; both the program and the verifier have no upgrade authority on devnet (checked).

Confirmed devnet fund and claim transactions with a real proof verification; wallet app, researcher CLI, encrypted findings, tests, 9-slide deck and video. No hosted demo; the expiry refund was never run on devnet; a proof takes about 18 minutes.
Clear relationship (bounty sponsor vs researcher) and named users; the README answers every judge question. Narrow: the demo bug is planted in bundled code.
Each new target needs a new guest program and deployment; proving is slow and needs Linux/Docker; writing the bug rule is hard for maintainers.
A zero-knowledge proof-of-exploit bounty that also encrypts the finding to the maintainer inside the proved computation is rare and well thought out.

projects.built_during_event: unclear: one squashed commit on 4 Oct; devnet deploy on 4 Oct 09:07 CEST
strengths: Trust-replacing logic fully on-chain; immutable program and verifier
Real proof verification and payout confirmed on devnet
Excellent answers on permissions, vanished parties and why blockchain
Proof bound to campaign, beneficiary and finding, so it cannot be redirected
weaknesses: Two compiled-in templates and one rule only
No hosted demo; heavy proving setup
Sponsor can read the finding from the pending transaction (disclosed)
projects.verdict: The most faithful answer to the brief: the payout approver is replaced by an immutable on-chain verifier, demonstrated on devnet, though narrow in scope.

scores.why: Both sides' collateral sits in a program vault, settlement is permissionless and a grace-period refund covers a vanished party; but the settler can pick any recent oracle price, even one from before expiry, and the program is still upgradeable.
Three full create-take-settle flows on devnet, a hosted app, video, deck and 28 program tests; marked down because the named repo is empty and the code lives in a pre-event repo.
Named users (Polish freelancers paid in EUR) and intermediary (bank FX desk), but the demo is EUR/USD in a test token and needs a counterparty with the opposite exposure.
Peer-to-peer liquidity and derivatives regulation are the real blockers; price not pinned to expiry.
An oracle-settled capped forward is a known DeFi primitive; the freelancer framing is the new part.

projects.built_during_event: partly: the named repo has no commits; the real code is in an older repo created 27 Sep, with escrow, backend and app shell pre-dating the event (disclosed)
strengths: Hosted app, video, deck and devnet settlements all present
No admin key over funds; anyone can settle
weaknesses: Settler chooses the price within a freshness window
EUR/USD test token instead of EUR/PLN for the named user
red_flags: The submitted repo has no commits
projects.verdict: Polished and deployed, but the oracle price is not pinned, the program is upgradeable and the repo situation is messy.

scores.why: Stakes held in program vaults; resolve, claim and refund are permissionless; results come from an oracle feed nobody signs for. But the admin creates each market, picks the oracle job and timings, and both programs are upgradeable.
A devnet market shows create, two bets, lock, oracle resolve and claim; 10 integration tests; the app runs locally. No video, no hosted UI, deck only as HTML.
Bettors who must trust a bookmaker are named and the bookmaker's powers listed; gambling carries heavy regulation and the yield angle runs on a mock.
Crowded market, a single free data source, one oracle sample, mock yield, licensing hurdles.
Pari-mutuel sports betting on Solana is a very common hackathon idea; the job-pinned oracle feed is the only distinctive part.
